new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive (no minimal pairs; phonemic status called uncertain) and is governed by vowel quality rather than by a fixed position: within the word-final VCV(CV)# window the first of the two syllables takes primary stress unless the second holds a 'stronger' vowel on the hierarchy /a/ > /i/ > /u/ > /o/ > /ɛ/, or a double-vowel nucleus (diphthong), which attracts stress. Concretely: monosyllables one primary stress; bisyllables stress on the stronger vowel, first if identical; trisyllables either medial stress or initial primary + final secondary; four-syllable words either second-syllable primary + final secondary or third-syllable primary + initial secondary; the one five-syllable word has primary on the fourth and secondary on the second. High pitch rides on stressed syllables (no pitch contrasts); phrase intonation overrides the word pattern phrase-finally.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress is assigned to alternate syllables both preceding and following the syllable with primary stress' (ED fn. 2, p. 91); illustrated in 6.2.2.1 (initial primary + second-syllable secondary), 6.2.3.2 (initial primary + final secondary), 6.2.4.1-2 and 6.2.5 (pp. 92-93). Only one primary stress per non-affixed word (6.3, p. 93).
new_statements.exceptions: The ED principle covers 'over 80% of all forms. The other 20% apparently includes loan words, compounds, and so on' (p. 91 fn. 2); 'Only a few examples have been found where this is not so' (6.2.2, p. 91); phrase-final position: intonation 'overrides the standard pitch and stress on word level' (4.3.1, p. 90) and the final syllable of a non-final phonological phrase 'bears stress, which, like pitch, may cause a change in the standard pattern of that word' (7, p. 94); vowel lengthening for emphasis (4.3.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Hepburn's data are from the Hiyewe dialect ('Syllable patterns which occur in Hiyewe', sec. 3.1, p. 86); the introduction (companion item rosettaproject_sny_detail-1) states that Saniyo Hiyewe has two major dialects, Saniyo (lower Wogamous / upper April) and Hiyewe (upper Wogamous), about 1000 speakers, Sepik Hill family. The statement applies to Hiyewe; no separate Saniyo-dialect stress data exist.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exception quote is present verbatim in the held archive.org scanned text at the stated sections/pages (4.3.1/4.3.3 p. 90; 6.2.2 with ED footnote 2 p. 91; examples p. 92); I additionally downloaded the page-image PDF and visually confirmed p. 91 (vowel hierarchy /ɑ/ > /i/ > /u/ > /o/ > /ɛ/, footnote '>80% of all forms'). (2) Deciding source: a primary SIL phonemic statement (phonology article, 15 pp) with a dedicated word-stress section; it is the sole published phonology of the language and the only Glottolog-listed work treating stress; no reference grammar, dissertation or instrumental study exists in Glottolog 5.1, the held OLAC index, or archive.org. The 'segmental' (vowel-quality-conditioned, non-contrastive, ~80% regular) coding follows the source faithfully, including its own hedges. (3) list of works to obtain is short
